speechtext:
Perhaps I should say a word or two in introducing this bill, which in effect is a simple matter. I have no doubt that it will commend itself to the committee, and particularly to the members representing Toronto constituencies. The Toronto harbour commissioners are the owners of land north of Fleet street in the city of Toronto. This land is bounded on the west by the Fort York armouries and on the east by lands leased to Rogers Majestic Limited. The lands owned by -the Toronto harbour commissioners comprise about six acres, but they have leased a portion of their lands at the eastern extremity to an important local firm, and have obtained demands from a United States industry interested in locating itself in Toronto for additional lands north of that which is already owned by them on the north side of Fleet street. The land they own has a frontage of approximately 1,321 feet along Fleet street, and there is a parcel north of theirs having an acreage of 3-4 acres. The Toronto harbour commissioners have negotiated with the owners thereof, namely, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, for the purchase of these lands.
The commissioners are of the opinion that not only in its own interests but also in the interests of the city of Toronto it is a wise

Toronto Harbour Commissioners
thing to purchase these 3-4 acres of land from the Canadian Pacific Railway company. The powers of the commissioners as constituted at present under statute are not sufficient to enable them to purchase the land. The object of the bill is to give them these supplemental powers, which in the opinion of the solicitors of the Toronto harbour commissioners as well as the solicitor of the city of Toronto are required to warrant the purchase of this additional land and the use thereof for the purpose set out.
The bill is a simple one; it has but two clauses: one, authorizing the purchase, and two, authorizing the issue and raising of debentures for the purpose of purchasing these lands.

Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill conferring authority upon the governor in council to authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to construct a line of railway from Bar-raute to Kiask falls on the Bell river, in the province of Quebec, a distance of approximately 55 miles at an estimated expenditure of $4,125,000 and an average expenditure of $75,000 per mile. speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM BARRAUTE TO KIASK FALLS, QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is to obtain authority from parliament to construct a branch line from Barraute, a point on the National Transcontinental railway, to Kiask falls on the Bell river. The projected line would be 55 miles in length, and it is situated in the Abitibi country about 400 miles north and west of the city of Quebec.
When branch lines of this kind are built the Canadian National Railways have a practice of considering the economic factors. In this, as in other cases, it looks first at the natural resources which exist in the territory to be served or to be tapped; second, at the cost of construction of the line, and third, at the traffic likely to be derived from the projected line. The railway has done that in this case, and has come to the conclusion

C.N.R.-Barraute to Kiask Falls

that the construction of this line would be profitable from the three angles I have just mentioned. I should like to deal with the three in a general way, but before doing so I want to make the statement that the cost of this line will be $4,125,000, which figure is arrived at taking the rate of $75,000 per mile.
Dealing with the development of natural resources in the area, the Canadian National Railways have obtained a survey, which was projected from an aerial photograph using the modern method of stereoptic vision, which enables the country to be seen in relief. This survey disclosed a number of very important features. It disclosed, first of all, the agricultural possibilities of that area. The territory to be traversed by this line lies in the clay belt area, and there is a very substantial area north of the Transcontinental railway in the valley of the Bell river suitable for agricultural purposes. The area west of the Bell river slopes gently to the north, and is heavily wooded; later I shall deal with the question of timber. The area to the east of the Bell river is rugged and rough, and is not suitable for agricultural purposes. The line would be capable of developing some
275.000	acres of arable land, and it would support an agricultural population of approximately 15,000 people, who would be engaged in farming and lumbering. In addition some 600 people would be engaged in other activities. According to the survey made at the request of the Canadian National Railways it would take some ten years before the full agricultural development would be completed.
This area has great colonization potentialities. The province of Quebec is planning an extensive colonization programme for the district, and a study has been prepared at the request of the minister of colonization of the province of Quebec by a committee set up by him, which has issued a report entitled "La Colonisation dans la Province de Quebec." This study was made by Mr. E. Min-ville, director of the school of higher commercial studies, Montreal, and contains some interesting conclusions which I do not want to go into fully, but perhaps I could summarize them by saying that the area to be served by this projected line has a double feature. First of all, it is the only one properly agricultural which has a bright future in the province of Quebec. Next, it is the only one which, even already partly populated, may be treated as a country to be built up.
Dealing next with the forest products of the area to be served, the line would tap huge pulpwood resources. In fact there are 700 square miles west of Bell river which
{Mr. Chevrier.]
contain some 4,700,000 cords of timber, and 240 square miles east of the Bell river which contain 1,500,000 cords of timber, in terms of pulpwood. Seven hundred square miles of this timber has been granted by the Quebec government to the Canada Paper Company, and it has been granted to the company because of the fact that the timber resources in the eastern townships of Quebec have become practically exhausted. Unless the Canada Paper Company is able to obtain resources elsewhere there is a strong possibility of its mills at Windsor Mills and elsewhere having to close down.
The total estimated timber in the 700 square miles which have been granted by the province to the Canada Paper Company is 4,480,000 cords, and the timber within the economic reach of the 43-7 miles of the line is 6,200,000 cords. The area to be traversed has, as well, mineral possibilities. The line traverses the main mineralized belt between Noranda on the west and the Chibougamau country on the east. The possibilities there are for gold, copper and zinc. In fact in that area are mines which have been prospected, which in the opinion of those who have prepared the survey have possibilities.

Yes. The policy of the railway, as I outlined in the beginning, is one which thoroughly investigates each branch line project. It investigates it as to the natural resources which will be opened up, as to the cost of the construction of the
C.N.R.-Banaule to Kiosk Falls

line, and as to the probable traffic which will result. Inasmuch as the total costs arising from the line are charged to the Canadian National Railways, including interest on the cost of construction as well as maintenance and operating expenses, the amount of new traffic which will be created from the development of additional natural resources has to reach a considerable figure to meet those costs. It has been the experience of the railway that when it can obtain a guarantee for the construction of the line in the earlier years, then the line is likely to be a paying project.
The Canadian National Railways has studied this project very carefully. It has prepared a survey, and it has obtained also from the records of the federal government, of the provincial government and from consultation of data in the hands of the Canada Paper, details of the natural resources in the country. It has convinced itself that this branch line would be in the interests of the railway as well as in the interests of the country. The board of directors have considered it carefully and after having given it the consideration which they give to all these lines have recommended in favour of it. speechtext:
The principle contained in this bill is the same as that which has been recognized in the Government Employees Compensation Act. The Government Employees Compensation Act, as the house knows, provides compensation for employees of the government who are killed or injured in the course of their employment, and that principle is one which has been recognized over the years and to which some extensions have been granted. During the war years there was granted an extension of that principle which provided compensation in the case of death or injuries to munition workers, and by extending the same principle to merchant seamen compensation is now being granted to those men where compensation is not already granted under the provincial statute.
The principle of workmen's compensation, which protects workmen and their dependents from loss of earning power due to accidents in their employment, is now generally recognized as the cornerstone of industrial welfare. During the war it was considered advisable by the government to bring in a measure providing for payment of workmen's compensation to seamen on Canadian ships who were not covered under the different provincial compensation acts. This was done
[M. Chevrier.l
under the merchant seamen compensation regulations, 1945, which were made under the War Measures Act and became effective on August 1, 1945.
The government, by virtue of this bill, now proposes to give statutory authority to these regulations. The bill provides, among a number of things, for the establishment of a workmen's compensation board consisting of three members,, and it covers first of all seamen engaged on ships registered in Canada or chartered by demise to persons registered in Canada when the ships are engaged on foreign or home-trade voyages. Second, if ordered by the governor in council, coverage may be extended to seamen engaged in Canada and employed in ships registered outside Canada and operated by persons resident in Canada or having their principal place of business in Canada, when the ships are engaged on foreign or home-trade voyages. Third, "seamen" includes all members of the crew but does not include pilots, apprenticed pilots or fishermen; and fourth, the bill does not cover seamen who are entitled to claim compensation under the Government Employees Compensation Act or any provincial act, nor does it cover seamen entitled1 to claim compensation under order in council P.C. 104/3546 of April 30, 1942, which provides protection for seamen suffering disability or death as a result of enemy action or counteraction taken against the same.

speechtext:
Yes. I believe it would cover that. Compensation is payable where there is personal injury by accident arising out of and in the course of employment. The only exceptions are: (1) Where the disability lasts less than seven days, and (2) Where the accident is attributable solely to the serious and wilful misconduct of the seaman and does not result in death or serious disability.
The question of negligence or absence of negligence of employer or seaman does not affect the matter, and the old legal defence of common employment and voluntary assumption of risk are no longer applicable. No agreement to forgo benefits of the act is valid and no contribution towards the benefits provided is to be collected from seamen. Compensation

Merchant Seamen
cannot be assigned, charged or attached without the approval of the board. The benefits provided are in lieu of right of action for damages against the employer.
Where the accident results in death, the widow or invalid husband is entitled to receive payment of $45 a month during widowhood, and if the seaman leaves children, she is also entitled to receive S10 a month for each child under eighteen, the children's allowance, in case of the death of the widow, being increased to $20. but the total monthly payment is not to exceed two-thirds of the seaman's average earnings, except that minimum compensation for the widow and one or more children is S55 a month. The widow is also to receive a lump sum of $100.
Where there is no widow or invalid husband, each child is entitled to $20 a month while under eighteen, but 'the total monthly payment is not in any case to exceed two-thirds of the seaman's average earnings. Where there is no widow or invalid husband or child, but there are other dependents, they are to be entitled to a sum reasonably proportionate to the pecuniary loss occasioned them by the seaman's death, but not in any case to exceed two-thirds of the seaman's average earnings. Where there are children but no widow and it seems desirable to continue the existing household, and an aunt, sister or other suitable person acts as foster mother in keeping up the household, the same payments may be made as if she were the widow.
There is special provision for invalid children over eighteen and for adopted children. Where the widow marries again, her own monthly payments cease on marriage, but she is entitled to a lump sum equal to two years' payments, and the children's payments continue as before. Necessary burial expenses not exceeding $125 are to be paid by the employer, and in addition transportation expenses of the body, from place of death to place of interment. not exceeding $125, are payable.
Credit is given for any payments made under the relative provisions of the Canada Shipping Act, 1934. In case of non-fatal accidents, a seaman who is totally disabled is entitled to receive two-thirds of his average earnings, disregarding any excess above $2,500 a year, but he is not in any case to receive less than $12.50 a week unless his average earnings are less than this amount, in which case he is to receive the full amount of his earnings. Compensation dates from the commencement of disability, but there is no compensation if the disability lasts less than seven days.
If the seaman is only partly disabled he is entitled to receive the same fraction of total disability allowance as his impairment is of
his full earning capacity. The awards for all permanent disability, partial as well as total, are in the form of monthly pension for life, except where impairment does not exceed ten per cent of total earning capacity, in which case payment may be ordered by the board in a lump sum.

speechtext:
I think I can give that figure as we go along. The compensation is on the basis of the seaman's average earnings but not including war service bonus paid under P.C. 149/2705.
The settling of the compensation is done in the following manner: All questions as to right to compensation and the amount of it are determined by the board and its officers, the procedure and methods adopted being as simple, speedy and inexpensive as possible. The board deals directly with the parties, and legal assistance is not necessary. The forms are furnished by the board.
With regard to medical aid, every seaman entitled to compensation is also entitled to medical, surgical and dental aid, and hospital and skilled nursing services, and is also entitled to prosthetic applicances. Any seaman receiving medical aid under the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, is not entitled to medical aid under the Merchant Seaman Compensation Act during the period and to the extent that he is receiving medical aid under the Canada Shipping Act.
Insurance provision: The scheme of the act is to require compulsory insurance to be taken out by employers to afford the necessary coverage. The cost to employers is thereby reduced to fixed amounts payable as insurance premiums. In the operation of the regulations the board has found that ship owners, with few exceptions, have been most cooperative and anxious to comply with the insurance requirements. The cost of administration will be charged to the employers on a basis to be determined by the board. The expenses of the board, which now consists of government officials serving without additional remuneration, are small.
The outstanding features of the bill are the simplicity of its provisions and procedure, the elimination of litigation and expense, wide protection for seamen and their dependents, immunity of the employer from individual liability, and the liberality of the benefits provided. I think the house will find generally that the regulations as covered by this bill are pretty much the same as those existing
Merchant Seamen

in the various provincial enactments. We have attempted to put in this bill the best that could be found in the provincial enactments. I am sure the bill will commend itself to the house.

subtopic: MERCHANT SEAMEN
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext:
I am sure there will be no disagreement with the general purposes of the bill. During the war we freely paid tribute to the services of the armed service personnel, but the men of the merchant seamen who served on the seven seas also deserve high commendation from the parliament and the people of Canada. In 1945 an order in council was passed providing for compensation for seamen who had been injured and for the dependents of the seamen who had lost their lives. As a matter of fact this party -would naturally give support to legislation such as this, because in 1942-and it was the first occasion on which the matter had received support from any political party-we went on record at the Winnipeg convention as follows:
The hazardous occupation of those serving in the merchant navy should be fully recognized and their interests protected by extending to them and their dependents protection in accordance with the principles expressed in these resolutions. The benefits of the Pensions Act as now applied to seafaring men by order in council should be confirmed by statute.
There are some provisions of the bill with respect to which I wish to ask the minister for further information. The first is the matter of transportation on the great lakes. Will this legislation be within the power of the dominion parliament? I express no opinion on it; I simply ask whether or not the question has been submitted to the law officers of the crown for determination.
The second point I wish to raise has to do with the multiplication of boards which parliament is asked to set up. During the war, when under the regulations and under order in council claims must have been much larger than they will be in the days of peace, it was not found necessary to set up another administrative body. It has not become necessary to set up an administrative body to administer the act providing for compensation to government employees. At a time when the people want us to reduce taxation, again and again provision is being made for the setting up of boards and the appointment of persons at large salaries- at least it generally turns out that large salaries are paid. Having regard to the small number of cases to which this act will apply,

I suggest there is no necessity of providing for a merchant seaman compensation board to consist of three members to be appointed by the governor in council. The number of cases to be dealt with will be so relatively small that within the department itself a temporary board could be set up to deal with them.
I now come to the sections dealing with the powers of the board. It is true that under the workmen's compensation acts of the various provinces the decisions of the board is final, but there has been a body of jurisprudence built up. I take strong exception to sections 17 and 18 which give to an administrative board, without regard to the justice of the case, the finality of deciding whether or not justice has or has not been done. Consideration should be given to the establishment of principles to govern the board. Until these principles are established there should be the right of appeal to the courts. This would not apply to every case, but the principle should be followed in the building of a jurisprudence or a set of principles to guide the board so that arbitrary and tyrannical rules once made may not become the basis of future decisions.
Finally, sir, I take strenuous objection to section 41, which is what I call snooper legislation. It provides that where it is found by the board, and mind you its decision is final- -that the widow to whom compensation has been awarded is a common prostitute or is openly living with any man in the relation of man and wite without being married to him, the compensation to such widow may be discontinued or suspended . . .
That type of paternalistic legislation indicates what I would term the snooper mentality. We had examples of it frequently during the period of the war when the recipients of allowances had investigations made from time to time with regard to alleged wrongdoing. I think this is the first time this sort of thing has been incorporated in a statute, however.

I am dealing with the principle of the bill, Mr. Chairman. I want to give an illustration of the arbitrary way in which boards have acted when they were not governed by legal principles; and I am going to refer to the workmen's compensation board of New Brunswick. In that province the words in the act are, "injury by accident". If a man receives an injury by accident he is entitled to compensation; but what does the board say? The board has ruled that for a man to obtain compensation he must suffer an accident, in the first place, and by reason of that accident he must suffer an injury. Let us say a longshoreman is lifting heavy boxes, or doing other heavy work, and suffers a rupture. He has suffered an injury, but the board says he is not entitled to compensation because there was no accident. There was not an accident, though he did have an injury. So for a longshoreman or any other workman to obtain compensation in such a case, he has to lie about the whole thing and say he turned his ankle, or fell; that he had an accident, and as a result suffered an injury. When they come before the board, in order to get the compensation to which they are entitled they have to lie about it; and they all understand that. This board may place a similar interpretation upon those words, and there is no opportunity for a seaman, as there is no opportunity for a workman in New Brunswick, to appeal. That opportunity did exist previously in New Brunswick, where the act provided that a man could appeal on a question of law but not on a question of fact. When the courts of the land, following the English decisions, held that the words

Merchant Seamen

"injury by accident" should be interpreted as they were in the English courts, the board had the act amended to provide that it should be the sole judge of questions of law as well as questions of fact. I submit that is altogether wrong, that a seaman as well as a workman should have the right to appeal if he feels the board is not treating him justly, and that right is taken away from him by this provision. It is my submission that a seaman, if he believes that the board has not treated him justly, should have the right of appeal. These boards are not infallible. I would ask the minister to give further consideration to amending that section.
I wish to refer also to section 29, which deals with insurance, subsection 1 of which states:
Every employer shall cover by insurance or other means satisfactory to the board, the risks of compensation arising under this act.
Does the board propose to insure these men, or do the ship owners insure their seamen with a private company?

speechtext:
I continue:
It was proved in evidence, on a claim by his widow for compensation, that this form of infection is hardly known to occur in this country except in coal-workings, that it is then due to infected rats in the workings, and that microorganisms causing the disease were found in rats caught after the workman's death in the section in which he had been working. From these facts the SheriiLSubstitute drew the inference that, although the manner in which the micro-organisms were transferred was not capable of proof, they were transferred to the workman from in-
[Mr. Hazen.l
fected rats in the colliery'. He therefore held that the "workman died as a result of injury by accident arising out of and in the course of his employment, the infection not being incidental to his employment, and awarded compensation.
The employers appealed from that decision, but it was held that the arbitrator was entitled to hold that the infection which produced the disease was an accident and that the disease itself was an injury by accident, within the meaning of the act. I cite that case to show how far the courts have gone in interpreting the words "injury by accident". In dealing with the facts in his judgment on appeal the Lord President said:
The real difficulty lies behind:	Was the infectious disease which culminated in the workman's death an "injury by accident" within the meaning of the act? It is no longer possible to dispose of this question in the negative on the ground (in itself unanswerable) that, in the ordinary use of language, nobody would describe a fatal disease-whether infectious or not-as an "injury by accident," or even as an "accident" at all. The situation must be accepted that, by a series of decisions, in which the turning-point was definitely reached by the decision of the House of Lords in Brintons, Ltd. v. Turvey (.1905) A.C. 230: 7 W.C.C.I., an infectious disease (not classed as an "industrial disease") may be "an injury by accident" within the meaning of the act.
If in the past under the order in council constituting the board it has ruled that a seaman who suffers from pneumonia cannot get compensation under the order in council which is now embodied in the bill, they may have made a wrong ruling. It must all depend on the facts of the case. Hon. members will find other decisions in the English courts; I have not had time to look them all up. When a man working in a pit, for instance, gets overheated and afterwards contracts a disease and dies from it, I think he is entitled to compensation, because that disease was injury by7" accident. I could go on and cite other cases but I do not propose to do so. I cite this one merely because I believe that the board may have misdirected itself if it held that in the case of pneumonia a seaman was not entitled to compensation. If it has misdirected itself I hope it will not do so in the future.
That raises another point. The board is supposed to get all the facts and decide the question on the facts, but when it comes to a question of law what experience have they to decide questions of law? They may decide them rightly or wrongly. In the case of a question of law I say that a seaman should have the right to appeal from the board's decision; if he feels that he is aggrieved he should have the right of appeal to one of the courts of the land.

speechtext:
I was not here this morning because I was engaged in other work and therefore I have not had an opportunity to say anything on this important bill. Merchant seamen for too long have been unprotected against injury. Some little time ago I had occasion to call to the attention of the minister the case of a young man of perfect physique who was injured in an accident upon a ship, in which he completely lost the use of his lower limbs. Though both the department of pensions and national health, as it was at that time, and the Department of Transport were very sympathetic in considering the representations I made, they were unable to obtain any permanent compensation in this case. So if only it will provide for cases of that kind I welcome this bill.
The point raised by the hon. member for St. John-Albert is important, but I doubt if it would be of any great value to the seamen if the employer has the same opportunity of taking the case to court when he is not satisfied. Then it would become a question, as I think it was before we had compensation acts, as to who has the longest purse. I believe representatives of labour and trade unionists generally have over the years, to my own knowledge as far as British Columbia is concerned, objected to having compensation cases reviewed by the courts. Even though they might be dissatisfied with board decisions, they would much rather have the cases dealt with by a board than have the act provide that, they might be referred to the courts. But of course a great deal will depend upon how the board is constituted. In the provinces I believe one member represents the employers, another represents labour and the third member is the chairman, who is supposed to be impartial. We have not yet reached the section setting up the board-it is the next section-but as I read it no provision is made for setting up a board of that kind. Of course what I am saying now is being said under the handicap of not having been here when the Minister of Transport spoke on the bill, but I would much rather have a board constituted as provincial boards are than have the seamen making appeals to the courts. I think what we should aim to do in this matter is to get a square deal for those concerned by keeping these cases out of court, and we should give that very serious consideration.

speechtext:
This is the section to which I made reference, which provides for the setting up of a compensation board. The
total number of cases in the year 1945-46 was some 177, and the minister pointed out that up to date the board had not been an expensive body 'because it was composed of officials of the various departments, together with a representative of the seamen. But that does not answer this question at all. This is a comprehensive section. Looking over the order in council I see that parliament is being asked to copy it almost in its entirety. I say "almost in its entirety"; the bill is a photographic copy, with the exception of section 3. At present the board which has been looking after these duties under this order in council is set up in this way:
-shall be a board to be known as the merchant seamen compensation board consisting of three members, namely, a chairman, a vice-chairman and a third member who shall be appointed by the minister, and who shall hold office during pleasure and serve without remuneration.
That is the wording of the order in council now. My hon. friend endeavoured to answer my objection to the setting up of another board by saying: Well, we are going to follow the same method that we have followed heretofore under the order in council. That is not what parliament is being asked to do. Parliament is being asked to pass section 3, subsection 4 of which reads:
A member of the board holds office during pleasure and shall be paid such salary as the governor in council may fix.
Now that is has been pointed out to the minister I am sure he will see the force of the argument, because here we are being asked to give the governor in council power to set up just another board. The governor in council can fix the salary at whatever they wish, and the person appointed holds office during pleasure. As a matter of fact, in regard to the setting up of boards and making the crown all powerful in this way I was reading something not long ago that makes it seem that history does repeat itself. I find that in the first thirty years of the reign of George III a resolution was introduced into the British House of Commons reading:
The power of the crown has increased, is increasing, and ought to be diminished.
That was about 1790. It was the famous resolution introduced by Dunning, of which I am sure the minister has heard. The only change necessary now would be to substitute "the executive" for "the crown" and that resolution could be introduced in this house; and with the support it would receive on the other side, being assured of the support of this side of the house, certainly that resolution would be passed to-day by this parliament. In view of the fact that it is not intended
Merchant Seamen

to set up a board to provide cushy jobs paying handsome salaries; since it is the intention to follow the procedure now being followed under the order in council, I suggest that subsection 4 of section 3 might be changed. I do not see why there should be this departure from an otherwise photographic copy of the order in council. It might be made to read: "A member of the board holds office during pleasure and shall serve without remuneration." Having regard to the fact that these three men were willing to serve last year, and that apparently they have expressed their willingness for the future, so there is no possibility of this act being used to bring about the appointment of a full board, I hope the minister will accept my suggestion. If he does not, I intend to have something more to say on it.

see no reason why we should make the provision here suggested. I have no desire to prevent the calling in of anyone under an arrangement whereby he shall receive a fair allowance for his time. speechtext: It seems to me that in view of the small number of cases involved, this is merely a departmental matter and could be done by one or two stenographers who would write letters to Vancouver, Halifax or some other point. speechtext: I was impressed by what was said by the hon. member for St. John-Albert with reference to the use of the word "accident". Cases have come before the courts in which two automobiles have been in collision, and the courts have decided that neither party is liable because it was an accident. "Accident" has two meanings. If the word "injury" were used instead of "accident", or if you used the two words, it would overcome any objection taken by any body constituted under this act, or by anyone else, that it is only an injury and not an accident. I realize that if this section is amended, many other sections will have to be amended also. An accident is something that no one can help, and perhaps we are insuring everyone regardless of whether injury is sustained through the individual's fault or otherwise. I have often thought that the word "accident" is a dangerous one. I suggest it should be injury. The question should be whether the man suffered injury. If that were the provision, the question of a man being injured by something that was not in the nature of external force would leave the matter open to be decided by the board. If he could prove conclusively that although he had not been struck by an external force he had acquired some disease as a direct result of his work, the position would be made clear. I can understand it would open the door to a man maintaining that any disease had been caused by his work when in point of fact it might not have been. I suggest that injury would be a better word, even if it has to be used in conjunction with the word accident.

speechtext:
I feel strongly that under this act if a seaman has not the right to appeal to a court on a question of law there will be cases in which he will not get justice. I have in mind certain cases under the workmen's compensation aot. I 'am thinking particularly of a girl who worked a machine by means of a lever. In the course of her work she injured her back. Perhaps some other girl working that lever would not have been injured, but this girl was, and it was necessary for her to have a surgical operation. The board said: "Yes; it is true she injured her back, but she is not entitled to compensation because there was no accident". Under the wording of the act there must be injury by accident. These people said: "We admit you had an injury and hurt your back, but you did not suffer an accident and therefore you are not entitled to compensation". If there were no appeal under this act-there Happened to be an appeal in the case I referred to

so far as any question of law vas concerned, the person who suffered might not have obtained justice. In the case I have mentioned, that girl could have obtained no compensation, and undoubtedly there will be cases under this act in which the board may make wrong legal decisions. This morning it was suggested that if a seaman got pneumonia he could not be entitled to compensation under this act. I submit there are cases under certain circumstances in which, if the word "injury" were used, the person affected would be entitled to compensation; and yet, if the board holds that he is not entitled to compensation, he can obtain none and he has no appeal. I feel strongly that he should have an appeal on questions of law, and therefore I am going to move that the words "law or" in the second line of section 18 be deleted, so that the section will read:
The decisions and findings of the board upon all questions of fact are final and conclusive.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: MERCHANT SEAMEN
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext:
I concur in what the hon. member for St. John-Albert has said. I have had experience of quite a number of oases that would come under section 18. Not so long ago someone came to see me, as many workmen do in Toronto. This person was working in a shell factory which was turning out small shells, perhaps a foot long and three inches in diameter. I do not know how much they would weigh, but one of these shells fell on the worker's foot from the height of the lathe. The chairman knows how high that would be. It injured the foot and the worker was incapacitated for a long time. The doctors of the board, after the

board had given this workman compensation for two or three months, turned the claim down flat. I have had in mind for some time bringing this matter to the attention of the public through some action that I propose through the medium of the Department of Labour. I have been seriously thinking of proposing that an act be passed enabling a workman to appeal from a decision of the board. There is no appeal to-day, so that when the board issues an order it is final and the workman has no more chance. I have come across several cases which have caused me to feel strongly on this point, because I feel that the workman should be given an opportunity to appeal from the decision of the board. I do not know to what body he would appeal-I am not a lawyer- but I suggest that, not the board, but a court should have the final say in case of a dispute, I want to back up what the hon. member for 8t. John-Albert has said.

speechtext: I am opposed to this amendment. I was in the legislature of British Columbia and had occasion to deal with hundreds of compensation cases in the lumbering industry, and I have heard a similar proposal discussed by labour organizations and by many individuals, some even who had received unfavourable decisions from boards. I must say, Mr. Chairman, my experience has shown me that there is general opposition from organized labour and from working people themselves to the principles enunciated in the amendment. In my opinion we would be wise to follow the practice of provincial boards.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: MERCHANT SEAMEN
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext:
I believe that wherever possible there should be one appeal, and that appeal should be to a court which would be reasonably accessible in each province. In Ontario in many cases the workmen's compensation board have given inadequate compensation. I shall give one example. Some years ago a man who had come from Nova Scotia and was working in a mine lost the partial use of one hand. The compensation board paid him $800, and he had to return to Nova Scotia. He could no longer be a miner; he had to return to the place whence he had come, with the opportunity of earning the money which he had previously earned absolutely gone. The sum of $800 would not go

Merchant Seamen
very far in repaying him for the loss of the use of his hand, as he had to make his living out of labour.
I should like to mention something which I overlooked. Suppose a man who is working on a ship which fishes for tuna in the southern Pacific leaves Vancouver on the ship, would he be a fisherman or a sailor? If he was a fisherman and was injured-and he would have good opportunity of getting injured on one of these ships-he would be entirely outside the act. I overlooked that example when the proper section was under discussion. I believe there should be one appeal, and I am quite willing to admit that it should be the appeal of the workman.
In Ontario the workmen's compensation board have a large fund. I would hate to tell how much has been gathered together. It is true that the employers are interested only in keeping down the claims so that they will not have a bigger assessment made against them. It is a sort of indirect way of protecting themselves. For some reason or other the board has not been particularly liberal with the workers. For that reason there should be one appeal.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: MERCHANT SEAMEN
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext:
A moment ago the hon. member for Davenport asked a question arising out of a portion of section 7, the disability section. The answer to that question is to be found in subsection 4 of section 24. I believe the hon. member for High Park is in favour of an appeal to a higher court, as is the hon. member for St. John-Albert, who moved the amendment.	The
answer to the questions can well be found in those who have had experience over the years in handling compensation cases. Both hon. gentlemen, who are lawyers, will agree with me that Ontario, more particularly, has gained a wide field of experience in that regard. The legislature of that province has seen fit not to include in the act a section giving the workmen, or for that matter the employer, the right of appeal. I have the workmen's compensation act of Ontario before me, and the language is as strong as, if not stronger than, the language used in the bill now before the committee. I think we would be well advised to take advantage of the experience gained by that province. In British Columbia there is no appeal from the findings of the board; there is no appeal in Quebec. So far as the question of fact is concerned there is no appeal in New Brunswick. I am not too sure whether I understood my hon. friend aright this morning, but perhaps he did say that that had been amended and that there was now no appeal in his own province of New Brunswick,
either on a question of law or on a question of fact. I think we would be well advised to follow the practice in these provinces, because in some instances, at least under the Government Employees' Compensation Act, we have to work through the provinces. I can think of some cases in which under that act the applications are made directly to the provincial boards and through the Department of Transport, handled by us but using the provincial board as an agency for the adjudication of these cases. I think we would be ill advised to change the section, particularly in view of the experience and practice over the years as I have indicated.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: MERCHANT SEAMEN
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext: No people have had greater experience in workmen's compensation matters . than the people of the United Kingdom, and there they have the right to appeal. I should like to cite another British ease. A man who was working sorting wool in a factory contracted a disease in the eye which blinded him. The wording of the act is "injury by accident." The board held that he was blinded while he was working in the plant, but they said that it was not injury by accident. The argument was that a bacillus which is found in wool had entered his eye and blinded him. The board said that that might be so, but it was not an injury by accident, and they so ruled. Under the British laws the workman had an opportunity to appeal and he did so. The case went to the House of Lords, they found that the man had suffered an injury by accident and was entitled to compensation. When you s'et up boards of this kind you gave them arbitrary powers and you take away from the people the right to appeal to the courts where justice is administered. If you do that you are doing a great disservice to them, and it does not make any difference to me whether the recommendation comes from a labour union or anybody else. The courts are set up to do justice, and if a man feels that he has not had justice done to him he should have the right to appeal to the courts.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: MERCHANT SEAMEN
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext:
I am well aware that labour unions are opposed to an appeal in the case of an injury to a workman. The same is true of industry, but I am thinking of the man who gets nothing. Where is he to get his chance? I have a case in mind, but I will not state in which province it happened because I am not in conflict with any workmen's compensation board. The man of whom I am thinking worked in a foundry, under pitched windows with nothing between him and the windows. It was a very cold room, and he caught what turned out to be
430S
Merchant Seamen

the cause of his death. He could not prove it. I went to see him just before he died. The board turned him down flat. In my judgment his death was the direct result of the conditions under which he had to work. He had no appeal. I am not finding any fault with any board. I quite agree that it would never do to allow workmen to have to face high-priced lawyers interested in the employers. If there was some place else to which they could go I do believe the workmen should have the right to go there. If this man of whom I speak had had a chance he might have obtained redress because the workmen's compensation board turned him down flat. When that is done a w'orkman has no further chance.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: MERCHANT SEAMEN
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext: I should like the minister to believe that what I am giving is the experience in Ontario. The people of whom I am thinking are the workmen, not the employers. This matter has not been lying dormant, by any means. It has been brought up in the legislature of Ontario, and very strong protests have been made in regard to it. It just happens they have not got around to amending the act, though I do not know why. There are many acts which need amendment, and this is one of them. 1 suggest that for the benefit of ,the worker one appeal should be allowed, and that to some judge, because I suggest that a judge would have a greater sense of his responsibilities than would most of the men who might be appointed to workmen's compensation boards, and we can trust a judge to do the right thing. There may not be many appeals, but there would be enough to satisfy the people, and perhaps redress some of the injustices.

speechtext:
But that is not the point I am making, whether it would cost much or little. I w'ant to refer to the case of Brintons Limited v. Turvey, which was decided in the British House of Lords in 1905. It must have cost something to take that case to the House of Lords, but it entirely changed the law as to the rights of workmen under the compensation act. If it had not been ftor that case and the decision of the House of Lords at that time, the workmen never would have obtained what they now receive under the workmen's compensation acts in Great Britain, and many other parts of the empire. That was the governing case, decided in 1905, and as a result for the last forty years workmen have been getting what they never got before. I should like to read the brief note on that case, to give hon. members a better idea of what it was about. It is taken from The English and Empire Digest, and reads:
While a workman was employed sorting wool m a factory a bacillus, according to the medical evidence, passed from the wool to the eye of the workman, and infected him with anthrax of which he died:	Held: this was a case of "injury
by accident" within the meaning of Workmen's Compensation Act, 1897.
That changed the whole law. From that time on a workman was able to get compensation if in the course of his employment he contracted a disease through a bacillus. Surely if it did cost something to establish that principle, it was well worth it. If it had not been for that particular case; if there had. not been the right of appeal, that board would be still holding that if a workman contracted a disease while at work he would not be entitled to any compensation at all.

I think that is a matter worthy of consideration.

speechtext:
Agreed.
(The opinion follows.)
I have to refer to your letter of March 18 enclosing for my opinion a copy of the merchant seamen compensation regulations. Your questions together with my answers thereto are as follows:
1.	Question:	Whether it is within the competence of the parliament of Canada to enact legislation incorporating the provisions of the merchant seamen compensation regulations, 1945?
Answer:	Yes.
2.	Question:	If your answer to question 1 is
in the affirmative, whether it is within the competence of parliament to enact legislation extending the provisions of the said regulations to cover the whole field of workmen's compensation for seamen employed on ships registered in Canada or operated by persons resident or having their principal place of business in Canada?
Answer: Yes.
3.	Question:	Whether it is within the competence of parliament to enact legislation extending the provisions of the said regulations to cover seamen employed on ships registered in Canada or operated by persons resident or having their principal place of business in Canada when such ships are engaged in voyages between any of the provinces of Canada or extending beyond the limits of any such province?
Answer: Yes.
4.	Question: Whether the legislatures of the provinces have power to enact legislation covering the subject matter of the said regulations in whole or in respect of seamen who are residents of the province and are engaged within the province to serve on a ship registered in Canada or operated by persons resident in Canada or having their principal place of business in Canada when such ship is employed in voyages between any of the provinces or extending beyond the limits of any such province?
Answer:	The privy council has held that
provincial legislation relating to workmen's compensation and applicable to seamen who are residents of the province is valid. As I read the decision, it was not restricted to operations within the province, nor to ships operated by persons resident or carrying on business in Canada. The legislation, however, was general in character applicable in the case of workmen generally.
5.	Question: In the event of a conflict between dominion legislation and provincial legislation covering the same subject matter as outlined in the above questions, which legislation would be inoperatitve?
Answer:	Dominion legislation would prevail.
The Deputy Minister, F. P. Yarcoe. Department of Transport Deputy Minister Ottawa.

I should like to make one observation and it is not to be taken as necessarily approving the terms of this resolution. I think one of the things that has struck the ordinary layman who has observed the work of the railways during the war was how the railways were able to carry on throughout the entire war period with so few accidents as actually occurred with the equipment they had. I was very much struck by the report which was made by the department not so long ago and which was in the hands of all hon. members, indicating that during the war period the ratio of accidents on the Canadian railways was actually less per person travelling than in the years prior to the war. That is a clear indication of what a grand job the railways did while the war was on, and that is no reflection, of course, on their work in time of peace.
On a previous occasion in this house I and other members have paid some tribute, as best we could in our humble way, to the work of the railway employees on the civilian front during the war. There was a great expansion in railway business during the war. That is on the records of this parliament in two or three sessions and I need not reiterate the details. I mention it only to point out that additional precautions must have been observed by the railways to do what, they did with so few accidents. Indeed, on the civilian front there were not many, if any better jobs done that that done by the railway workers in Canada, particularly when we bear in mind that there was not the time or the opportunity or the materials for them to repair and overhaul their rolling stock as they would have done in the more leisurely peacetime period. I am not surprised that both the major railway companies in Canada
are now taking steps to put their rolling stock in shape and pick up the slack which inevitably occurred during the war.
I take it that this $9,000,000 is required not only for new equipment but for the repair and overhauling of the old equipment.
I am told also that some of the roadbed throughout the country is badly in need of ballast to bring it up to its normal peacetime condition. It was not possible to do that during the war because of the shortage of manpower and materials. In making these observations, I believe that I am expressing the reaction which most laymen feel to the railway situation as they understand it. I do not. pose as an expert on railway matters; far from it, but I did wish to pay this tribute to the railway companies and to the railway workers who made it possible for the railways to carry such a tremendous load during the war with such speed and dispatch and with so few accidents. I do not suppose any of our railway workers, had you asked them in 1938 or 1939 if the railways could carry the increased number of passengers and increased freight tonnage which they did carry during the war, would have thought that it would be possible for the railways to do it, with such efficiency and with so few accidents.

Probably no one had a better opportunity of realizing the handicaps under which they carried on this work than one who has spent the greater part of a month each year in travelling between Victoria and Ottarva and finding out what the men have to do. When you see a workman on his back under a car fixing up the steamline when the temperature is 40 degrees below zero, and he finally gets you away on time in such weather, you have an appreciation of what the men on the Canadian railways have done for the people of Canada during the past six years, and I am sure they will appreciate very much the references that have been made to them by the hon. member for Peel.

I should like to ask the minister some questions, and if the information is not now available, perhaps it might be given when the bill is before us. What prompts me to ask these questions is that in normal times the Canadian National Railways shows a deficit. It has been suggested that one of the reasons for that is its heavy capitalization and its large bonded indebtedness. It carries such a load in that respect that never except in war years can it show figures in the black; they are generally in the red. I wondered whether it would be feasible to write down the indebtedness of the Canadian National Railways in so far as it is held by the government, because it seems to me that we are fooling ourselves. If the Canadian National pays all its surplus into the government anyway, so that the country gets the benefit of any surplus earnings, simply because those earnings do not cover the amount of the bonded indebtfMr. Maj'hew.]
edness we show the system in the red. If that is the case a change could easily be effected and it would not do us any harm, whereas it would have a salutary effect on the morale of the railway, both employees and management. That was what I had in mind and what prompts me to put certain questions, the answers to which I shall be glad to get if it is at all possible for the minister to give them to-day. If he cannot let me have them now he can do so at a later time. The questions are these. How much of the outstanding liability of the Canadian National is held by the government, and how much in the hands of individual bondholders? The second question is this:	How much did the Canadian
National Railways actually pay into the government during the war years, in the form of surplus earnings as profit? What profit did it show and pay to the government or into the consolidated revenue fund in the years of the war? Third, was any of those profits used to pay off bonded indebtedness or was it all absorbed in reducing previous deficits which had been charged up, or what was the final disposition of it?

Mr. DAVID A. CROLL (Spadina): Mr. Speaker, I intend to take the opportunity of saying a few words on this particular bill because it deals with the matter of trade, and particularly foreign trade. To-day Canada is faced with the greatest opportunity for obtaining foreign trade that it ever had. Hon. members know that there is a world-wide hunger for all kinds of goods, manufactured as well as raw materials, and that two important exporting nations, Japan and Germany, have been put out of business, probably for our generation. In addition to that, all the European countries, once the source of much of the world's low-cost consumer goods, have had their manufacturing plants either impaired or dislocated by the war. Not only have we the traditional consumer countries like South America starving for goods, but even producer countries which have not been able to get their war-stalled industries running are crying as never before for goods, and looking to the remaining industrial countries such as Canada to provide them. At the same time I point a note of warning that already some of the (European countries are in the export market. Holland is already in the market in the West Indies. Some of them are recovering even
Commercial Corporation

more quickly than we expected. Belgium is having a quick recovery. At the present time Canada stands in a unique position. Here we have an industrial plant untouched by the ravages of war and expanded to the point where we are one of the foremost industrial nations of the world. We have not only prewar industries; but we have stepped up tremendously our new industries, new processes, and we have increased our productivity more than the most optimistic person would imagine possible. Added to this, we have the good will of the entire world. The world knows that it can trust us and do business with us.
I think I understand Canada's present foreign trade policy. It is as follows, and I think I can best bring it to the attention of the house under four points. The first is to meet our commitments abroad; the second, to police exports of certain goods, for example, aeroplanes and uranium; third, in the case of goods which have a bearing on our internal economy, for example, those on which there are domestic subsidies, to see to it that the subsidies are repaid before the goods are sent overseas; and fourth, to maintain adequate civilian supplies for Canadians. I do not think I go too far when I say that the policies of this department will determine to a large extent whether we prosper or stagnate economically during the years immediately ahead. It is a department with enormous responsibilities, but also one which is indeed very well run. For a number of reasons it is a department which must find it difficult to plot its actions too far ahead. It has to find markets for Canadian goods, and if conditions in those markets change suddenly because of foreign competition, it must be in a position to meet that competition and secure the markets for Canada. What we can agree on is that we, as a nation, must export more goods than we ever did before or else we stagnate economically. We have just experienced a period of full employment because of the war. We know that Canada's industrial capacity has been tremendously expanded. None of us suggests that our present population can consume the products of our enlarged industry. There are those of us who advocate increased immigration, but we who favour that policy are not so naive as to believe that the results we seek can be immediately achieved. In the interim we have to sell abroad the products and the surplus that we have in our domestic market; and I suggest, in addition to the goods which are surplus to our domestic consumption, some of the products which are in domestic demand at the present time.
We have always relied in this country upon exports to give our people jobs and profits

and a reasonably good sort of living. In the past twenty years exports have meant S10 a month to every man, woman and child in the country; or to put it another way, $650 to every farm in Canada. These figures come from the current letter of the Royal Bank of Canada, which I commend to the attention of hon. members. This is an approach to the problem from the long-range, or twenty-year aspect. That was not so serious a problem so long as our economy was based on the production of foodstuffs which the world must have in order to eat and to live. But the war has brought a fundamental change to Canada and I doubt whether we can regard ourselves any longer as primarily an agricultural country. In making ourselves what we like to boast of as the arsenal of democracy, we built up a problem for the future, the problem of distributing the output of our greatly expanded industrial plant. The same factories which built the vehicles, the weapons and all sorts of military incidentals for half a dozen nations besides our own obviously were too big in peace time for merely domestic production. Therefore we cannot accept as our present needs either the quantity or the composition of our pre-war exports. We have to become major suppliers of manufactured goods as well as of foodstuffs and minerals. We have to do so if we are to maintain production and employment and satisfied stomachs and well clothed backs. We can no longer simply strive to continue that $10 per person a month that the Royal bank reports as the twenty-year average; we can no longer accept the one-third of our dollar which the department advertises as the surprising fraction of our individual income which derives from export trade. At least one of our best known economists sets the figures at 40 per cent rather than at 33% per cent. That it has to be high is unquestioned except by those of the most unconventional economic views. Most of my C.C.F. friends will agree, I imagine, with their British socialist colleagues who have given the expansion of exports No. 1 place on their economy programme. Admitting then, as most of us do, that exports must be increased we can surely proceed to the further admission that it must be done in a hurry. International competition is not such that it will wait a gradual and painless adjustment of the Canadian economy to the drastically new set of conditions. Rather the adjustment must not only be abrupt but may be even a little painful if it is to achieve its purpose.
What must we do then to get our share of the world's markets which we so urgently require? I think the house will -agree when I say we must first produce. Then I call atten-

tion to the fact that there is no production from an idle factory; there is no production for export in the midst of an industrial struggle as bitter as Canada has ever known. There is no production for export when labour and management are locked in the throes of a long-term battle for and against upward revisions of wages and consolidation of contractual agreements and working conditions. There is no production for any purpose when a plant is closed tight by a strike, and we may as well face the fact that the strikes we have to-day are perhaps but preliminary to a wave of walk-outs, against which neither the government nor management has advanced any effective, constructive policy.
There are three parties to production: management, labour and the investor. I find myself unable to criticize those who provide the funds for industry. The banks and trust companies, .to say nothing of the well-heeled private investor, are eager to give their support to ventures in foreign trade. The institutions I have just mentioned have devoted a great deal of their advertising and publicity to an endeavour to create export-mindedness among Canadian manufacturers, but as far as the other parties to industry are concerned there is an attitude which I may be permitted to call unenlightened self-interest. They are shutting their eyes to the fact that by suspending production to-day they are eliminating opportunities for export to-morrow. Management has not been too greatly concerned with strikes in its plants when, in that appallingly significant phrase it likes to use, "it has been working for Ilsley". You hear this often, and I challenge anjmne to suggest a more complete confession of the absence of social responsibility.
Labour, on the other hand, has failed to appreciate that the picket line at the closed plant to-day may well be the forerunner of a jobless to-morrowr. Anj'one who has looked objectively at the industrial picture in Canada over the past six years would know that of necessity there would be an adjustment of wages, hours and working conditions after the war. Grievances piled up during the period when most unions were being faithful to their no-strike pledge. Living costs have risen in spite of the government's commendable effort; and there is reason in the personal experience of all of us to believe that advance has been greater than the percentage indicated by the indices maintained by the Department of Labour. Wages have to be increased; improved working conditions have to formalized by contract. Surely, with an appreciation of this fact, so apparent to anyone
who is not a party to either side of industry, the transition should have been achieved without the serious stoppages we have undergone in the past year and which we have not yet settled. Management started out by offering nothing in response to the workers' demands, by obeying only the letter of our improved labour laws, or by skirting those laws entirely. They challenged labour to do its work and, labour having done so, they capitulated but passed on none of their new-found wisdom to their colleagues in industry. So strike has followed strike; defeat has followed defeat for management. Nevertheless each industry faced, with the problem continues to act as though its own were the very first strike to be faced by any member of the Canadian Manufacturers Association. The thinking of management in reference to labour has been in a vacuum. If management approached business deals with as little know-how as it approaches labour problems, management would soon be retailing the apples which the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank) so actively promotes in this house. On the labour side the picture is also disheartening.

speechtext:
I doubt that very much. I was over there for four years, under pretty difficult conditions. They were not starving, and they put up a pretty good show in the end. We know markets are waiting for us, but at the present time not only are exports being hampered by the policy-and more [Mr. Croll.l
power to it-of supplying necessities to the war-torn countries of Europe, but our efforts are being nullified by a deep concern for the demands of the domestic consumer. This is stated to be one of the major considerations for dictating a continuance of the law requiring that any man who exports must, in the majority of cases, obtain an export permit from the government. My suggestion is that we earmark a certain percentage of all our productivity for export, so that when permits are withheld the suggestion will not be well founded that they are unreasonably withheld.
We still in this country, a land of plenty, respond with outraged screams to any suggestion that we might do with the second best for a while, if we have to sacrifice at the present time. I merely point to some of the newspaper comment, even in to-day's newspaper, where people in this country become extremely hot under the collar when they find out that some of our shirts are in both Jamaica and Trinidad. To many of us a natural contrast occurs. We might think of the well-to-do Englishman in his shabby suit, and perhaps in his frayed collar. We think of his satisfaction at the news that the best materials in the world, goods that he manufactures, are selling well overseas, although, of course, he is unable to obtain them. To him austerity has become a temporary way of life from which he expects to get dividends in better living at some time in the future, whereas to us austerity is just another word to look up in the dictionary.
We think of how pleased the ordinary Englishman must be to know that his ruined country was able to lift those exports from 33 per cent of the 1938 average last year to 95 per cent by quantity of that average in the first quarter of 1946. The goal is 75 per cent above the 1938 average. And, having trebled the total of exports in one year, he is well on his way to trebling them again in the next twelve months. He can do that only by forgoing the thing he would like to eat, that he would like to drink, that he would like to wear. My guess is that he will do it. I point out to the house that it is much easier to buy an English-made suit on King street in Toronto than it is on Saville row in London; and it is several times easier to buy a drink of "Scotch" on St. Catherines street, Montreal than on Princess street, Edinburgh. So I suggest that in our present crisis our government might well demand greater sacrifice from the people of Canada by way of a willingness to forgo luxuries in favour of future prosperity. If it is adequately

Commercial Corporation
explained to them I do not think we would any longer find Canadians outraged when the minister reports that shirts they have a hard time in buying can be bought in Jamaica or Trinidad.
Our government might well lift export restrictions on goods urgently desired in countries willing to embark upon long-range trade agreements with Canada. Inevitably they will enter into such agreements with our competitors, if we cannot immediately undertake delivery.
I believe the house will agree that we must take our markets where we find them. While before the war three-quarters of Canada's exports went to Great Britain and the United States, only about ten per cent found their way to the far east. By confining ourselves to those two countries, we neglected Australia, New Zealand, India and China with a combined population of well over half a billion people, a most fertile field for trade development. As a result, this area, much of which comes within the scope of empire preference, was left to others to exploit. For example, the United States was able to secure much of the foreign trade which otherwise would have been diverted easily to Canada. With the disappearance of Japan from this field, a great share of the foreign trade becomes vacant, so to speak, and our goal in post-war trade. expansion must be to fill that vacancy with Canadian goods.
The LatinnAmerican market, about which much has been said lately, has many characteristics such as are typical of present-day conditions. There are great opportunities for trade in those countries. Yet we must not deceive ourselves into thinking that huge profits are there for the taking, or firm markets a certainty. To consider LatimAmeriea as an export field, the position is that almost every country, in marked contrast to the prewar condition, has a good deal of spare cash on hand. With the closing of the German and Japanese sources, there is a great demand for almost every type of goods. But many South American countries are controlling this demand by restricting rigidly the volume and type of imports. There is no intention of squandering on luxuries their wartime accumulation of foreign exchange. In view of the very low standard of living in South America, many standard articles in Canada are considered luxuries to nine-tenths of the people in South America.
I began by saying that, first of all, we need production. Then, as suggested, we need a diversion of a larger share of that production to export trade. The third recommendation 63260-272
is that, as Canadians, we learn a little more about world trading. We have not been very good at it in the past. We still labour under the delusion that if a line of goods is not saleable at home, it might as well be dumped on the world market and be sold there.
