I am told it has been a general rule, although those on the west coast, and also on the east, are possibly somewhat more foreign trademinded than are those of us in the rest of Canada.
Over the week-end I had a discussion with a few important manufacturers in Toronto, and discussed exports with them. Their view was that they were in no hurry about making any excursion into foreign markets, that in due time Canadian producers, having met domestic demands, would step in, cut prices a few cents, and capture whatever market appealed to them. I am sure the house agrees with me that that is a childish view. Does anyone think that without a knowledge of the taste, opinions, prejudices, and a thousand-and-one local factors in any given overseas market, anyone can step in and snatch it away from world traders who have been studying that market in detail for perhaps a hundred years?
It is a matter of record in the department that not long ago a Canadian manufacturer, taking advantage of a new entree into a west Indian market, took a chance on ignoring detailed instructions and shipped a cargo of materials in styles and colours which, from what he had read, he was sure would appeal to the negro inhabitants of the island. It so happened that these negroes traditionally abhorred the colours and styles of that shipment. Naturally it did not sell.
I ask the house this question: Where does Canada stand in respect of future sales on that island? Canadian firms have lost overseas business because they refused to appreciate that their treasured trade mark was a bad-luck symbol in the countries to which they were shipping goods. One exporter from Canada insisted upon having on his carton a tiger with a short moustache, when he had been told that a tiger must have long whiskers. As it turns out, a tiger with a short moustache in many parts of the east is considered a bad-luck omen. The result was that his goods did not sell until he met the specifications.
It is also a matter of record that another Canadian manufacturer allowed $2 million of business to go to British and Swedish companies because he could not understand why

Commercial Corporation

people of that particular country preferred his product with a hole for a handle rather than with a fitted handle. Of course the answer was that they liked it that way. It is our business to meet their wishes.
The real basis of foreign trade, in addition to meeting style and other requirements, is to deliver the goods. Before we can do that we must produce. The world has to be told what kind of goods we manufacture and what kind we can deliver. At the moment they do not know, and perhaps there are even some hon. members who are not fully acquainted with the goods we are able to manufacture and export. Many countries are unable to think of Canada except in terms of bacon, cheese and wheat. The world generally does not know that we can sell anything from tooth brushes to aeroplanes, that we have to offer a large range of commodities which includes such diversified products as oilcloth, machinery, chemicals, earthenware, sporting goods, whisky and locomotives. The world must be told of these things, not only through booklets which at best have a limited appeal, but through extensive advertising in newspapers and magazines. Here I should like to commend the department upon the able advertising that they have carried out, not only in Canada but in other countries. I think that advertising should be extended. When the estimates come up we should take the opportunity to give the minister all the money he needs in order that he may sell Canadian products abroad and let people in other countries know that we can produce goods and deliver them.
I said a few minutes ago-one hon. member did not agree with me-that education is required at home about the importance of foreign trade and the possibilities of venturing in futurities. Most people are paying attention to domestic markets. It is natural to want to do business with people whom you know and with whom you live. A great demand exists in the domestic markets; there are profits to be made here, so they say, "What is the use of looking elsewhere?" But the domestic market, as we have seen, cannot absorb more than two-thirds of our production. If we mean to maintain peak production- and that is the only way our standard of living will remain as it is or go higher-then we must sell our surplus products. As the present time this may be difficult because some commodities are badly needed right here at home. However, we can fill these home needs little by little without losing any business in the long run, whereas foreign markets which lie open to us to-day will be gone in a year unless we are prepared to make a strong bid [Mr. Croll.j
for them now. If some goods are in short supply in this country, a token shipment will at least keep our foot in the door, but we must act quickly.
We owe our present standard of living to the fact that our exports in 1945 were valued at S3,125 million, or more than a third of our national income for that year. Unless we maintain peak production and peak distribution of goods we cannot hope to go on improving our standard of living. I know that people in Canada are hungry for goods, but there must be some sense of proportion in the matter. The policy of all for us and nothing for other countries will give us a very shortlived prosperity indeed. In a year or two our domestic needs will be met and then, when we look abroad in order to sell our surpluses-by the simple arithmetic of population we can see that there will be surpluses before long-we shall find the markets of the world spoken for by others and we shall be frozen out.
In dealing with this particular bill our course is clear. We have to produce as we have never produced before. We have to go short on some things for a while and, most important of all, we have to stop bickering and get down to producing. Canada to-day has a tremendous opportunity, the opportunity of a lifetime, an opportunity which will never be here again, and we must seize that opportunity now.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) said that our industries were untouched by the ravages of war. That may be true; but during the war, because of shortages and a lack of labour, our industries lost many of their foreign markets. I am afraid that in some cases they have lost them forever. Many of those foreign countries, when they found that they could not secure the goods that we had been exporting, subsidized their own industries to manufacture what we used to export to them in peace time. Therefore it is necessary that the Department of Trade and Commerce find new markets for those exports which we have lost. I know the minister is quite familiar with the situation, and I am hoping that he will take the proper steps to try to find markets for these goods. In checking over this bill, I find that it has not a time limit and I think it should have one of not more than two years.
When the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) was speaking on one of the items standing in his name he mentioned that one of the branches of his department, the Canadian information service, would

Commercial Corporation
advertise Canadian goods overseas. The hon. member for Spadina referred to advertising and said that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) should be given all the money he wanted for the purpose of advertising Canadian goods. I do not know about giving the minister all the money he wants, but I think he should be given sufficient to do this advertising, and the Department of Trade and Commerce should do the advertising, not the Canadian information service. I have absolutely no faith in the Canadian information service and very few people in Canada have.
Not long ago the minister paid a visit to the South and Central American countries. During these last few months, we have reaped the benefits of his trip. By going to those South and Central American countries he created a better feeling among the people there. I believe, if the minister would visit other countries from which he thinks we could get trade, it would create prestige for this country and help Canadian manufacturers to increase their exports. I noticed an item in the Commercial Intelligence Journal of August 3, 1946, under the title "Foreign trade service", which reads:
The foreign trade service, whose function is the maintenance and promotion of trade between Canada and other countries, consists of seven divisions as follows:
And further down:
Export division: Consists of a group of commodity specialists, in direct contact with Canadian industry, who supply information and render assistance with respect to the particular commodities or groups of commodities for which they are responsible. It includes the export permit branch in order to ensure the coordination of its work with the issuance of export permits so long as these wartime controls remain.
When we are in committee I should like the minister to tell us how that division will fit in with the Canadian Commercial Corporation; also how the import division functions. Personally I feel that the Canadian Commercial Corporation should emphasize exports and forget imports for the time being, because the wartime prices and trade board lifted prices on exports and the exports that are going into other countries from Canada are often not goods needed by them but are luxury goods. What we need now is what the people want to wear and what they need to carry on their everyday business. I have a lot of questions to ask when we get into committee.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard a lot about exports from the hon member for Spadina (Mr. 63260-272J
Croll). I should like to have heard something about imports at the same time, because surely foreign trade means trading, not merely exports. If we are not going to receive imports in exchange for our exports we are simply giving our goods away. I never could see the point in trying to force our goods into a country which can very well make those same goods for themselves. Unless we are prepared to receive back goods for the goods we export, it seems to me that we cannot raise our standard of living. We may work harder, but at the same time we shall have to tighten our belts. I do not think there can be any argument against that.
The case for Great Britain is different. In the first place, they are dependent very largely on foreign countries for the raw materials they need. In the second place, Great Britain has incurred tremendous debt owing to the war, and she needs credits in order to obtain the raw materials which she can process and export as finished goods. But those conditions are not Canadian at all. Ours are the reverse. We have plenty of raw materials, and we have no external debt to speak of.	[DOT]
It seemed to me, as I listened to the hon. member for Spadina, that what he really has in mind, the real export he was thinking of, is unemployment. Let me say this, that no country wants to import unemployment, and that is why tariffs are raised against imports. We say that it is fundamental to the social credit way of thinking that a country should export only what it cannot consume, in exchange for those things which it cannot produce. That is trade in the real sense of the word.
We do have certain things in Canada that we produce largely in excess of our needs, and of course wheat is one. On the other hand, there are things which we cannot produce and never will be able to produce commercially-all tropical fruits, for instance. These things we never can produce in Canada, by commercial means anyway. But we do have plenty of basic products which we produce in excess of our needs and which we can export in exchange for the articles which we can neither grow nor produce for ourselves.
There is one point with regard to our trade relations with South America. I understand that the attitude adopted ait the San Francisco conference, where the people of the Argentine were told bluntly that they were not wanted, has not improved their relations with either the United States or with us. I understand that that was done to please Soviet Russia. In the meantime, as one might have supposed,
Commercial Corporation

Soviet Russia has slipped in and established a full-time ambassador in the Argentine and has largely gained the trade which was formerly enjoyed by those countries which told the Argentine that she was not wanted. It is just another example that we would do well, with, regard to all countries, to mind our own business and let other countries mind theirs. That works well in any community. As long as people mind their own business there is peace, but 'as soon as they start to mind other people's business there is likely to be trouble and it is pretty soon coming.
I should like to hear some of the speakers who follow me say a few words about imports in exchange for our exports, because the idea that we can raise our standard of living in Canada by exporting our goods on long-term credits is not true. One reason for that is that if the goods are exported and are not traded for a corresponding amount of imports, and the wages stay in this country, then there is inflation, and that has to be taken care of by increased taxation. So, as Major Douglas said years ago, Ithe only thing that the working man will get out of a favourable balance of foreign trade is a longer work day. We shall have to work harder, tighten our belts, and pay higher taxes for the privilege of doing it.

Mr. Speaker, I shall take only a few moments. In fact, I had not intended to say anything on this bill until the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ctoll) opened up in the way he did. I have always considered that a country like Canada, with the nature of our production, should have a vigorous export policy, but I have always contended thalt the first charge upon the production of any country is a decent standard1 of living for those who make that production possible. The first charge on the production of any nation is the opportunity for the people who make that production possible to use that production to give them a decent Standard of living. As the- hon. member for Wetaskiwin- (Mr. Jaques) has pointed out, very little if anything was said about import business. My associates and I have at all times contended that, while we must have export markets for surplus products, we should in turn have a policy of vigorous import business in exchange for those surpluses, so that our people can round out a full standard of living by having the use of things they cannot economically produce or manufacture in this country. In other words, you can have a vigorous export market, and continue to have it and have your people happy at home only, if you make your inter-

national 'trade a two-way street. The hon. member for Spadina spent altogether too much time on the edge of that street, going one way and not giving any thought to the other side of the street.
When the hon. member suggested that a certain portion of our production should be earmarked for export I was absolutely astounded. I was astounded to hear it coming from that part of the house. I could have understood it if he had put it a little differently. I am- prepared, and I am- sure the majority of the Canadian people are prepared, to have belts tightened, to do without some of the things we ordinarily have and should have, so long as they go to those parts of the world that are urgently in need of them. But that is, we hope, only a temporary condition. That is a matter which needs to be dealt with only on some occasions. But when you are speaking of international trade and suggest that we should earmark a certain proportion of our production for export, regardless of whether or not our own people have enough of the things so produced-well, simply to be polite and to have my words remain parliamentary, I will say it is just so much hooey.
When I first looked over the bill I thought it was a fairly good one. I thought it was making some provision whereby we could foster both our export and our import business. But after listening to the hon. member for Spadina I am beginning to have my doubts. I am wondering whether his speech this afternoon is an indication of what the government intends to do with this bill, and I suggest that during the dinner recess we consider that question seriously before supporting the bill. If that is Liberal policy; if it is what the Liberal government intends to do with this piece of legislation, I for one will give it serious thought during the dinner recess.
Before I sit down, may I say this. Let no one go from this chamber and say that I am opposed, or that my associates are opposed, to sending as much as possible of our goods to countries that are at present in dire need of them. Let me, however, also say this. I simply cannot understand the attitude of a government which at one time throws out the call for the people of this country to give all they can in order to prevent starvation in some countries, and then at the same time allows machines to be shipped to other countries, which possibly cannot use those machines at the present time, in order to help relieve the situation in Europe, while in our own country we have a crop standing there in need of machines to take it off. Even when they turn some of these machines over

The Argentine Nation
to UNRRA, I would point out that the people in need of food cannot eat agricultural implements. They need the food that we could harvest with those implements, and that food would tide them over their present plight. This export business can be something that is absolutely idiotic at times, something that is beyond all reason when carried to extremes.
So far as Latin America is concerned, I have no love for the Argentine, any more than for others, and as the hon. member for Wetaskiwin suggested, possibly they have thrown their business somewhere else. But I would say to him and to other hon. members that there was a time, not so very long ago, when the Argentine was found wanting, when much more was at stake than a little bit of export business. In spite of what the hon. member for Spadina said, I still do not think his speech was an indication of Liberal policy.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. J. A. MacKinnon (Minister of Trade and Commerce) for the second reading of bill No. 251, to establish the Canadian Commercial corporation.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the house for more than a few minutes. We want, however, to put our reasons for supporting the principle of the bill on record as clearly as we can. We supported the principle of the bill when it was before us in the resolution stage, and although I have not had an opportunity of checking it over section by
Commercial Corporation

section as carefully as I should like, from the study that I have given it I see no reason why we should withdraw our support now.
We support the bill, first, because in our opinion it is an attempt not only to expand our trade but also to bring about orderly marketing. No matter how reluctantly we may approach this question, I am convinced that circumstances will push us forward and that this may well be the first step toward setting up export and import boards. We should not be afraid of that because it has been done before.
When I spoke on the budget I said in reply to the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) that the government was basing its hope for a return to prosperity on export trade. At that time I pointed out that the only necessity for a country to export was in order to import, and I am glad to note that the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Jaques) has read my speech, as was indicated in what he said just before recess. I say that, not boastfully but because I had never heard the case put in this house in the way in which I put it in my budget speech and in the way the hon. member for Wetaskiwin put it this afternoon.
This country, of course, is interested in exports. But if we are to export for long we must also be interested in imports. There are many things which our people need which we cannot produce here. Some of the commodities that we produce here are better produced in other places. I like to look at good workmanship and good materials because it is pleasing to the eye. I think a good piece of workmanship is akin to art, even when it is a useful article such as clothing, china and things of that kind. I am quite satisfied that there are many people in Canada who would like to buy some of the beautiful woollen goods produced in Great Britain, perhaps better than in any other country in the world. Unfortunately they cannot often purchase them, but they would like them just because almost every' one likes good quality. I know that people in Canada w'ould like to buy some of the beautiful china which Britain also makes. There are many things which are beautiful to look at, a joy to handle, and pleasing to have about. There is no reason why we should not have more of these things. I believe men and women are better men and women if they have beautiful things about them to look at. These are some of the reasons why we should be interested in trade, in buying and selling, exchanging the things we have in abundance for the things that we have not at all. If we can do that, our standard of living will be raised.

This afternoon some hon. member mentioned the matter of the loans we have made since the end of the war. I am not disturbed about these loans even if we never get value for them, because we came through the war in good shape, and most of the people, or perhaps all of the people, to whom we made these loans suffered greatly. But there is another reason, namely, that the quicker we restore the economy of these countries, the better off we shall be ourselves. Therefore, so far as I am concerned I shall support measures of this kind for some time to come. I hope we shall get a return some day, and I hope we shall be able to accept that return in goods which our people can use. We should not ask for it until the people to whom we lent the money or perhaps our goods can pay for them without hurting themselves.
I am quite aware of the fact that in the sort of economy in which we live, a capitalist economy, export trade is a necessity even at times when the masses of the people who produce the goods are in need of them. In such instances goods must be exported because of the maldistribution of the income which went into circulation in the production of those goods. That, however, will have to be taken care of in some other way, so that our own people will not be in want, while the things they could use must be exported because the people who could buy them can not consume them. For these reasons, wdiile the house may be as critical as it likes of sections of the bill, in its general principle I think we can support it as a measure that helps to meet the needs of to-day. Perhaps a few years from now conditions will have changed and wye shall require something else; but at the moment, if this is as far as the government feels it can go, I see no reason why the bill should not have our support.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I asked the minister a few questions before recess. I wonder if he would answer them now.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
To begin with, I want to thank the hon. member for Peterborough West for his comment on the bill and on the work of the department generally. One specific question the hon. member asked was the relationship of the Canadian Commercial corporation to our foreign trade service. In asking that question, I believe the hon. member was particularly anxious that there should be no overlapping or conflict in the

Commercial Corporation
work of the two organizations. The foreign trade service of the department continues its promotional activities, continues its search for new markets, making connections and so on. It has, however, no capacity to consummate actual transactions which are desirable but which cannot be handled by private traders. The normal follow-through on its promotional activities is and should be carried on by private traders. The Canadian Commercial corporation will not initiate new trade, but is available as a necessary piece of machinery to carry out certain types of transactions. It is purely of assistance to private trade, not in any wTay a competitor.
'Mr. FRASER: Will the minister comment on the suggestion I made with regard to a time limit?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
The corporation is
being established to fill a definite need created by war conditions and tire special problem of transition to more normal trading relations. That need exists to-day -and will probably continue for some time. The future of the corporation will depend in large part upon the degree of freedom in private trade accorded to the nationals of ex-enemy countries. The corporation will be continued' in existence as long as necessary to assist private traders.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Has the minister any idea how long thait will be?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: It depends on so many things. For instance, it depends on how long Japan might be occupied by the victorious allies, or how long Germany might be occupied. It is impossible to state any actual time limit, bult this organization is being set up as an aid to business and will be continued just as long as, and not longer than, it will continue to be a necessary aid to business.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: As long as it is useful?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: As long as its usefulness lasts. It has not been established to subsidize exports or imports, or to replace private traders in any way.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Will the minister say what extra staff he has to take on to handle this work, and also whether this new corporation is taking on men or women for advertising or publicity work?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
The Canadian Commercial corporation has taken over the staff of the Canadian export board, the organization that carried on this work during the war. It has taken over that staff in its entirety, as I understand it, and in addition it has engaged four men who have had unusual experience in work of this kind. The staff has all been
recruited through the civil service commission, according to my information, with the exception of these senior officials. The intention is to continue that practice. The four experts I just mentioned, the senior officers of the organization, were recruited through the Canadian export board. They are men who had formerly been with munitions and supply, the wartime prices and trade board and possibly other departments.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: What is t'he total staff at the present time? What is the staff in Canada and what will it be in foreign countries? I imagine you will have agents in foreign countries, or do the trade commissioners act in that capacity?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: At the present time there is a staff of approximately 115. At the moment it is not intended to appoint any agents in foreign countries. In some cases use is being made of existing trade commissioner services in those countries.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: They should1 be able to handle this work in those foreign countries, should they not? You should not need to send any extra help there for that purpose.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: It depends entirely upon the nature and volume of work that may arise, but it is not our intention to set up any organization in addition to what we now have unless we find it necessary to do so. In reply to the question concerning advertising, I may say there are no arrangements or plans at all for any advertising in connection with this corporation.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: What part does the Canadian Commercial Corporation take in deciding what goods are to be exported from Canada? For exiample, we learn that Canadian shirts are being exported to the United States. Is the Canadian Commercial Corporation involved in that offence, or just what is its position?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: The Canadian Commercial Corporation will clear with the appropriate administrator or controller as to whether or not merchandise can be properly exported.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Which one of these governmental bodies decides at the present time whether shirts are to be exported from Canada?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: That is the result of conversations between the men in charge of supply in Canada and t'he officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Who are the culprits? Who are the controllers who reached that decision?
Commercial Corporation

Which branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce is involved in the decision? Is it the Canadian Commercial corporation or some other branch of the department?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: The Canadian Commercial corporation has nothing whatsoever to do with it. I do not wish to start a long discussion on the point, but-

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Shirts are hard to get.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: In response to a question to-day by the hon. member for Eglinton I tabled a return showing the number of shirts and other wearing apparel produced in Canada, and the number exported. The number exported is only a small fraction of the production.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Where are the shirts, then?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: The great shortage in Canada is in the kind of shirts the hon. member for Davenport wears.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I cannot get one at all.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I have the same difficulty the hon. member has. That is something he will have to ask the producers.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: What fraction is exported?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Keep your shirt on.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I haven't got one. They export them all, whether we 'have any or not.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: This matter has nothing whatsoever to do with the corporation under discussion. But the hon. member for Bow River will have a proper answer if he calls for the return I laid on the table to-day in answer to a question by the hon. member for Eglinton.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Could the minister give the fraction?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I believe it is a fraction of one per cent.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I understand that the Canadian Commercial corporation has nothing to do with the decision as to what goods are to be exported?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: When the resolution preceding the bill was in committee we asked the minister why it had not been possible for the Canadian export board to carry on, instead of a new crown company being set up. He promised to make an answer when the bill was in committee. Will he do so now?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I am glad to do that. The government was urged to match the facilities afforded British and American traders by the United Kingdom Commercial corporation and the United States Commercial company. A government board which has to act in the name of His Majesty is not a practical medium through which to carry out foreign trade transactions, such as buying or selling a particular parcel of goods. Further, it was the experience of the Canadian export board that many firms preferred to do business with a company which could sue and be sued, rather than with a department of government.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I am not clear as to what functions this company can perform that our trade commissioners cannot perform. Is there not likely to be some duplication?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: There is a mistaken idea that the trade commissioners representing Canada abroad are commercial travellers, and that they actually sell goods. That is not their function at all.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Do they not solicit trade?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: They seek out buyers in foreign countries-not so much individuals, although they would do it in that way-for merchandise in excess production in Canada. They do not sell a bill of goods, at all. They merely bring the buyer in a foreign country in touch with the vendor in Canada.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: What is the relationship between a trade commissioner and the Canadian Commercial corporation? "Will these commissioners operate independently, or will they be servants of this organization?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Actually there is no connection at all between our Canadian trade commissioners service abroad and this organization. As I said earlier, it may be that we may use their services to a slight extent in some foreign countries. But there is no duplication of service there; there is no conflict of service. It is not our intention to have any overlapping.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Earlier in the evening the minister said that we were going to use certain of these trade commissioners to carry on the work of the corporation.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
I referred to the statement I had made earlier in the evening when I said it was possible that we may make use of our trade commissioners abroad in connection with this. But that has not yet been decided.

Commercial Corporation

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: How will the staff of the corporation be disposed of when its work is completed?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: The staff at present have the status of temporary civil servants only. I imagine, when the time comes, they will likely be absorbed in other branches of government, or in private industry.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Is the corporation going to do any advertising to sell goods?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Is the corporation not 'being set up to seek to deal in a big way, not in the direct sale of surplus goods, but between one government and another, or between one large buyer and a large vendor?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Would the meat pro-produced from the horses on the prairies around Swift Current not be sold through this corporation?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES

On section 2-Definitions.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Will the corporation be set up in the present offices of the export board?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I should like to ask a question in connection with subsection 4. I notice that as directors there are a representative of the Department of National Revenue, customs and excise branch, a representative from industry and one from fishing. However, I see no director representing agriculture. Why is there no representative of agriculture on the directorate?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Agriculture has its own facilities for handling this sort of thing; the meat board, for instance.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: The deputy minister of fisheries is mentioned.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
What about British
Columbia apples?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
They are not marketed through a government agency. In answer to 63260-273
the hon. member for Comox-AIberni, the deputy minister of fisheries was shown when the bill was drafted because he was an employee at that time. However, he will have to be replaced.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Purposes.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I notice in paragraph (b) (ii) it is provided that the corporation is established to dispose of goods and commodities that are available for export from Canada. I think I am correct in saying that there are very few manufactured products now available for export; they are mostly natural products; am I correct?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Yes, I think that is correct.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
I think there are many manufactured products that might be made available for export now in small quantities. I realize that there are tremendous demands for manufactured products in Canada and that there are many export companies able to sell these products in foreign countries, but they are prohibited from doing so at the present time because of the shortages that exist here. I am going to advocate that some of our manufactured products be made available for export in small quantities so that new markets can be opened up. There are plenty of markets all over the world crying for consumer goods and, if we will do in a very small way what Great Britain is doing in a large way and deny ourselves just a little bit more, we shall open up channels of communication for the export of manufactured articles to many countries to which we have never sold before. I am going to advocate that, despite the shortages which exist, the Department of Trade and Commerce should follow a truly liberal policy in the granting of export permits in order to develop new markets. I think such a policy would return large dividends to this country in the future.
There is one other thing I should like to bring to the attention of the committee and the minister. UNRRA has been buying in bulk from Canada, so I am told, and is taking the whole of our production in certain lines, which leaves nothing available with which to open up new markets. I am told also that other countries with which UNRRA is dealing are selling only a part of their production, which leaves some available for export. I have not this information on good authority, but I think it is something we should guard against. If we are to continue to sell to UNRRA in order to help the people of

Commercial Corporation

Europe, I do not think we should sacrifice the whole of our export surplus. We should not be asked to do more than other countries are doing in this connection. We should still leave ourselves some surplus for export. Are the markets of the British empire being opened up to Canadian goods? Is there any conflict with the mother country, or are we able to compete with the mother country on an equal basis?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
In concluding his
remarks, the hon. member has asked a most difficult question. The United Kingdom is doing everything in her power to establish an export trade, and in seeking export markets we are naturally in competition with the United Kingdom as we are with the other great trading nations. I do not think the United Kingdom is making it any easier for us than is any other country.

On section 5-Powers.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Paragraph (c) refers to the storing and processing of goods or commodities, either as principal or agent. Storing is all right, but I object to the processing of goods by this corporation and I think that should be deleted.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES

I expect we do, but in the ordinary storage of the fish steps will have to be taken to see that that frozen state is maintained. I am quite familiar with the handling of fish in the part of Canada from which I come, in this country north of Edmonton. Large quantities of fish are exported in

a semi-frozen state. I can quite conceive where that state would have to be maintained in any intermediate storage plant.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Would not "storing" be broad enough to cover that?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I do not think so, no.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: "Storing and packing" would be all right. I think the minister should change it because it is too broad.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that there is no intention whatever of invading any manufacturing field.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Russia is in the market for machinery for heavy industrial plants, and I know a company in Toronto that makes just the kind of machinery they are after. Would it be part of the business of this corporation to bring buyers in Russia or the government in Russia in contact with the producer of such machinery in Canada?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Not necessarily to bring them together. If they were together and needed this kind of machinery to complete the deal, it would be available.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Would the minister expand a Little more about this freezing of Edmonton fish because I did not quite understand it?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN DEVELOPMENT OF TRADE WITH OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: The fish that I have in mind from the lakes north of Edmonton are shipped in a semi-frozen condition to the markets in Chicago and New York. They are shipped in great volume, and it was the maintenance of a proper state of freezing to which I was referring.

subtopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM-AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION

speechtext: Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister) moved the second reading of bill No. 301, respecting a succession duty agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom, signed at London, in England, on the 5th day of June, 1946.

subtopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM-AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
I am not sure whether the minister has made a comprehensive statement with reference to the subject matter of this bill, but if he has not done so either on the resolution or at some other stage, I suggest that before second reading is given he ought to make that statement.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I understand that a comprehensive statement was made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) at the resolution stage, and I had 'hoped it would be sufficient to state at this time that the bill is to give legal effect to an arrangement entered into between the government of the United Kingdom and the government of Canada to avoid, if possible, duplication of succession duties. There are quite a large number of provisions in the agreement, all designed to avoid payment of succession duties both in Canada and in the United Kingdom on the same property, and that required agreement of the contracting parties to determine a great many questions respecting which decisions had not been the same in the two countries.
The situation which gives rise to a possibility of double taxation is where the decedent resides in one country and dies leaving property in the other. When it is tangible property there is not too much difficulty, though there may be double taxation; but even when there is a desire to avoid double taxation, if you do not follow the same principles for the purpose of determining where is the legal situs of the property you do not achieve the result. Therefore it was necessary to examine carefully the whole situation and agree upon rules which would apply in both jurisdictions to determine the situs of property and to determine in what jurisdiction it could be taxed and what credit would be given in the other jurisdiction when the tax was paid.
I think all hon. members would agree with the desirability of an arrangement of that kind. As hon. members know, there is a similar arrangement between Canada and the United States which was sanctioned by legislation passed by this parliament in 1944. In the general desire to facilitate trade and to eliminate obstacles which prevent that freedom of choice in setting up commercial establishments or branches thereof it is desirable to avoid this doubling of taxation. It is serious enough to have to pay them once, and I think all will agree that it is desirable, in order that these tax laws may not prevent the interchange of investment, to strive toward a goal of avoiding double taxation. This agreement was entered into for that purpose, and the legislation which is submitted to parliament is for the purpose of giving it legislative sanction; because, of course, there has to be legislative sanction to avoid the application of the taxes imposed by statutes in the two countries.
The bill gives legislative sanction to the agreement and if it is desired explanations can be given in committee as to the various clauses of the agreement and the reason for each one of them. I would hope on the principle that we would all agree that we were striving toward a desirable goal, and that the only criticism could be upon the effectiveness of the clauses to reach that goal. That could be more conveniently considered or explained at the committee stage.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.

The duties which are the subject of the agreement are m the United Kingdom, the estate duty imposed by the United Kingdom, and in Canada the succession duty imposed by Canada. It was well realized by the government of the United Kingdom that there were also succession duties imposed by provincial governments to which this would not in terms apply; but there was the hope that it would be a good example which the provinces might find it to their advantage and to the advantage of their respective citizens to follow.

I think it is the same in British Columbia. I believe there is empowering legislation under which the executive government may make an arrangement, and when it is made it operates by virtue of the empowering legislation. I am informed that even with respect to this agreement there will not have to be special legislation in the United Kingdom; that the finance statutes of the United Kingdom authorize the chancellor of the exchequer to make agreements of this kind, and that they can be made effective under order in council without further enactment by the United Kingdom parliament. But here there was no special enabling legislation. My experience over the last few years has been that it was preferable to come to parliament and say just what one 
wanted to have confirmed rather than to ask parliament to give one blanket authority in advance.

speechtext:

speechtext:

Succession Duties

Mr. ST. 'LAURENT: It might be helpful if I were to give hon. members this statement which has been prepared respecting article III. Clauses (a), (d), (h), (i), (j), (k), (1), (m) and (n) are thought to be a repetition of the common law rule.
Clause (b) deals with the situs of negotiable bills of exchange and negotiable promissory notes, and with the situs of property in transitu.
It has been held in England that bills of exchange and promissory notes do not alter the nature of simple contract debts, and these debts are situate in England if the debtor is resident there. On the other hand, the Supreme Court of Canada has recently decided that negotiable instruments are subject to duty if found in Canada. Clause (b) now makes a uniform rule applicable in the determination of the situs of all negotiable instruments, namely, that they are to be regarded as situated where they are found at the time of the owner's death.

subtopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM-AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
Is that a special rule?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No, that is a rule which has been agreed upon in deference to the decision of our supreme court, though it is contrary to what was held previously in the United Kingdom in respect of several of these instruments.
With regard to property in transitu the rule in England has been that where property is in transit to that country at the time of the owner's death it is situated there. In a recent Ontario case, however, this principle was not applied in the case of property in transit from Ontario to the United States. Clause (b) now makes a uniform rule applicable to the situs of this class of property.
Clause (c) provides that all debts, whether secured or unsecured, shall be deemed to be situated at the place where the debtor was resident.

speechtext:

The hon. member knows that simple debts were deemed to be situate where the debtor resided, but that a debt evidenced by an instrument under seal was deemed to be

situate where the instrument was found. The agreement provides that that distinction will not exist. A debt, whether under seal or not, shall be deemed to be situate at the residence of the debtor.

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister) moved the second reading of bill No. 300, respecting an income tax agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom, signed at London, in England, on the fifth day of June, 1946.
He said: Mr. Speaker, a statement was made on this bill by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) at the resolution stage. The aim of this bill, like that of the one we have just passed, is to avoid duplication of taxation on the same income. I think the only way to get a clear idea of how the two governments have hoped that they might achieve that object is by going through the agreement itself article by article. I think it would be more convenient to have that done at the committee stage than for me to give any lengthy explanation on the second reading.
Motion agreed to, bill read a second time
and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
